notes.summary: Venn diagram questions use circles (or other shapes) to show how groups are related. Either you pick the diagram that fits three class names or some statements, or you read numbers from a diagram and add the right parts. Check one pair at a time: is one group inside the other, do they overlap, or are they apart?

concepts.title: The three relations
concepts.body:
Any two groups are related in exactly one of three ways:
RelationPictureExample
One inside the otherSmall circle inside a big circleMangoes and Fruits
OverlapTwo circles that crossWomen and Doctors
ApartTwo circles that do not touchCats and Dogs

With three groups there are three pairs (1–2, 2–3, 1–3). Decide each pair, then find the diagram where all three pairs match.

concepts.title: Common three-group patterns
concepts.body:
Most questions use one of these eight pictures. Learn one example for each:
  • One inside another: Kolkata, West Bengal, India.
  • Two apart, both inside a third: Cats, Dogs, Animals.
  • Two overlapping, both inside a third: Females, Mothers, Sisters.
  • One inside another, a third crossing both: Mothers, Women, Doctors.
  • All three overlapping: Women, Doctors, Singers.
  • Chain, the middle group meets both ends: Indians, Singers, Americans.
  • All three apart: Pens, Cows, Rivers.
  • One inside another, the third apart: Kittens, Cats, Tables.

concepts.title: Use real-world facts here
concepts.body:
Unlike syllogism, Venn class questions use everyday knowledge. Ask simple questions for each pair: "Is every X a Y?" "Can some X be Y?"
  • People and their roles overlap: a woman can be a doctor, a singer and a mother.
  • Men and Women, Boys and Girls, Fathers and Mothers are apart.
  • Things and people are apart: Doctors and Hospitals.
  • Places nest: city inside state inside country inside continent. A city cannot be in two countries.
  • Relations nest by gender: Fathers inside Men, Mothers inside Women; Fathers and Brothers overlap.

concepts.title: Reading a numbered diagram
concepts.body:
Each number belongs to one region. Name the regions carefully:
  • Only A: inside A, outside every other shape.
  • A and B but not C: the A–B overlap outside C.
  • A and B (no "only"): the whole A–B overlap, including the centre.
  • Exactly two: the three two-way overlaps, not the centre.
  • At least two: exactly two plus the centre.
  • A but not B: every part of A outside B.

Mini example from the figure: singers and actors = 4 + 3 = 7; exactly two groups = 5 + 7 + 4 = 16.

concepts.title: Shapes standing for groups
concepts.body:
Some diagrams use a rectangle, a circle and a triangle instead of three circles. The method is the same. For each number, ask three questions: inside the rectangle? inside the circle? inside the triangle? Then match the description.

In the figure (rectangle = graduates, circle = teachers, triangle = women): women teachers who are not graduates = 4; graduates who are neither teachers nor women = 12.

concepts.title: From statements to a diagram
concepts.body: Draw each statement as its basic picture: "All A are B" puts A inside B, "Some A are B" makes them cross, "No A is B" keeps them apart. Choose the option that matches every statement and adds nothing that is not stated. Example: All cats are animals. No animal is a plant. Answer: cats inside animals, plants apart from both.

concepts.title: Formulas for counting sets
concepts.body:
• A or B (at least one) = A + B − both.
  • Neither = total − (A or B).
  • Only A = A − both.
  • Three sets: A or B or C = A + B + C − (AB + BC + CA) + ABC, where AB means "A and B" including the centre.
Mini example: 40 students, 25 like tea, 20 like coffee, 10 like both. Tea or coffee = 25 + 20 − 10 = 35, so 5 like neither.

varieties.name: Best diagram for three classes
varieties.how: Decide inside, overlap or apart for each of the three pairs, then pick the diagram that matches all three.

example.q: Which diagram best shows Snakes, Reptiles and Poisonous creatures?
steps: Snakes and Reptiles: every snake is a reptile, so Snakes sits inside Reptiles.
Snakes and Poisonous: some snakes are poisonous, so they overlap.
Reptiles and Poisonous: they overlap, and some poisonous creatures (scorpions) are not reptiles, so Poisonous also goes outside Reptiles.
example.answer: A small circle inside a big one, with a third circle crossing both

varieties.name: Numbers in a circle diagram
varieties.how: Shade the regions the question describes, then add only those numbers. Watch for "only", "but not" and "exactly".

example.q: In the figure, how many people are actors but not singers?
steps: Actors but not singers = the parts of the Actors circle outside Singers.
Actors only = 15. Actors and dancers, not singers = 7.
15 + 7 = 22. (4 and 3 are also singers, so leave them out.)

varieties.name: Shapes standing for groups
varieties.how: For each number, check inside or outside every shape, then pick the region that fits the description exactly.

example.q: In the figure, the rectangle stands for graduates, the circle for teachers and the triangle for women. How many women teachers are not graduates?
steps: Women teachers = inside both the triangle and the circle.
Only one region is inside the triangle and circle but outside the rectangle: it has 4.

varieties.name: Diagram for given statements
varieties.how: Turn each statement into inside, overlap or apart, draw only that, and match the option.

example.q: Select the diagram that represents: All pens are tools. Some tools are toys. No toy is a pen.
steps: All pens are tools: Pens inside Tools.
Some tools are toys: Toys crosses Tools.
No toy is a pen: Toys must not touch Pens.
example.answer: Pens inside Tools, with Toys crossing Tools away from Pens

varieties.name: Counting with two or three sets
varieties.how: Use A or B = A + B − both, then Neither = total − (A or B).

example.q: In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket, 28 play football and 12 play both. How many play neither game?

tips: Check all three pairs, not just two; most wrong options get one pair wrong.
Use everyday facts in class questions (a mother is always a woman), but not in syllogism.
"Only" means a single region; without "only" the overlap includes the centre.
Exactly two = the three side overlaps; at least two = those plus the centre.
For shapes, test every number against every shape before choosing.
For set problems, write A + B − both first; "neither" comes last.
traps: Men and Women (or Boys and Girls) never overlap, so they are never drawn crossing.
A group that belongs fully to one class can still cross another class: Doctors cross Women and Mothers.
In "A but not B", the A–C overlap outside B also counts.
Do not add the centre twice when you add the three overlaps for "A and B".

questions.q: Which of the following diagrams best represents the relationship between Mothers, Women and Doctors?
questions.solution:
Every mother is a woman → Mothers inside Women.
Some women are doctors and some mothers are doctors → Doctors overlap both.
Diagram (c) shows a small circle inside a big circle, and a third circle overlapping both.

questions.q: Which of the following diagrams best represents the relationship between Dog, Animal and Cat?
questions.solution:
Dogs are animals and cats are animals → both inside Animal.
No dog is a cat → the two small circles are separate.
Diagram (d) shows this.

questions.q: Study the diagram. How many people are singers and dancers but NOT actors?
questions.solution:
Singers ∩ Dancers, outside Actors = the region marked 5.
(The 3 in the centre are also actors, so they are not counted.)

questions.q: Study the diagram. How many singers are also actors?
questions.solution:
Singers ∩ Actors = the region with 4 (singer and actor only) + the centre 3 (all three).
4 + 3 = 7.

questions.q: Which diagram best represents the relationship between Graduates, Teachers and Unemployed persons?
questions.solution:
Some teachers are graduates and some unemployed persons are graduates → Graduates overlaps both.
A teacher has a job, so no teacher is unemployed → Teachers and Unemployed are separate.
Diagram (b): a middle circle overlapping two circles that do not touch each other.

questions.q: Study the diagram. How many people belong to exactly two of the three groups?
questions.solution:
Exactly two groups = the three overlap regions that exclude the centre.
Singers–Dancers only: 5; Dancers–Actors only: 7; Singers–Actors only: 4.
5 + 7 + 4 = 16.

flashcards.back: Pairwise overlaps only, not the centre
